subject: science

items.q: Which of these shows a chemical property of an element?
items.correct: Magnesium burning brightly in air
items.misconception: Gallium melting in a person's hand
items.why: Ask: is a new substance made? Melted gallium is still gallium, and it turns solid again when it cools. Only a reaction, such as burning, shows a chemical property.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.random_wrong: Iodine crystals dissolving in ethanol

items.q: Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature. All three are in Group 7. What does this show?
items.correct: Elements in one group can be in different states
items.misconception: These three cannot really all be in one group
items.why: Similar is not identical. Look for the trend going down a group: a steady change in melting point, state or reactivity.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.random_wrong: Their single atoms are a gas, a liquid and a solid

items.q: The chart shows the melting points of four metals. Which statement does the chart support?
items.correct: Two of these metals melt below 100 °C
items.misconception: All four of these metals are solids at 20 °C
items.why: Mercury is the exception: it is shiny, conducts electricity and is a metal, but it is a liquid at 20 °C.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.random_wrong: Each of these metals has a high melting point

items.q: How did Mendeleev put the elements in order in his table?
items.correct: By atomic mass, keeping similar elements together
items.misconception: By atomic number, as today's table does
items.why: Mendeleev ordered the elements by atomic mass and moved some where needed to keep similar elements together. Atomic number came later.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.random_wrong: By atomic mass alone, with no swaps made

items.q: The diagram shows part of the periodic table with today's atomic masses. Mendeleev put tellurium (Te) before iodine (I). Why?
items.correct: To put iodine with chlorine and bromine
items.misconception: He made a mistake with their order
items.why: For Mendeleev, properties came first: atomic mass set the rough order, and similar properties decided each element's group.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.random_wrong: He was ordering by atomic number

items.q: Mendeleev left a gap in the group with silicon and tin. What did he expect the missing element to be like?
items.correct: Similar to silicon and tin in its group
items.misconception: Like the elements on either side in its row
items.why: Look down a column for similar elements. Across a row, elements change from metals to non-metals.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.random_wrong: Identical to silicon and tin in every way

items.q: Argon, the first noble gas to be collected, was found in 1894. Where were the noble gases in Mendeleev's first table, made in 1869?
items.correct: Nowhere: his table had no place for them
items.misconception: In Group 0, just as in today's table
items.why: Scientific models change as new evidence arrives. Argon, the first noble gas to be collected, was found in 1894, after Mendeleev's first table, and the noble gases needed a new group.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.random_wrong: In the gaps he had left for them

items.q: In the periodic table, what is a period?
items.correct: A row of elements going across the table
items.misconception: A column of elements down the table
items.why: Groups go down, like a family tree; periods go across, like a line of writing.
items.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: A family of elements that react alike

items.q: The diagram shows an outline of the periodic table with one column shaded. Which statement about the shaded elements is correct?
items.correct: They all react in a similar way
items.misconception: They are all gases at room temperature
items.why: Check each element: Group 7 alone has gases (fluorine, chlorine), a liquid (bromine) and a solid (iodine).
items.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: They form one period of the table

items.q: What does the staircase line on the periodic table separate?
items.correct: Metal elements from non-metals
items.misconception: Reactive elements from unreactive ones
items.why: Reactivity is not a metal-only property: the halogens are reactive non-metals, and the noble gases are unreactive non-metals.
items.specStatementText: the periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: Solid elements from gaseous ones

items.q: Potassium is below sodium in Group 1. Bromine is below chlorine in Group 7. Compared with the element above it, how reactive is each?
items.correct: Potassium more; bromine less
items.misconception: Potassium more; bromine more
items.why: Learn each group's trend separately: Group 1 gets more reactive going down; Group 7 gets less reactive going down.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.random_wrong: Potassium less; bromine less

items.q: Rubidium is just below potassium in Group 1. How will rubidium react with water, compared with potassium?
items.correct: More vigorously, as it is lower in the group
items.misconception: Less vigorously, as the top one reacts most
items.why: Check which group it is: going down Group 1 reactivity rises; going down Group 7 it falls.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.random_wrong: Just as vigorously, as it is in one group

items.q: The diagram shows how hot iron wool reacts with three Group 7 elements. Fluorine is above chlorine. Predict how hot iron wool reacts with fluorine.
items.correct: Even more strongly than with chlorine
items.misconception: Nothing can be said without a test
items.why: A prediction uses a pattern; a test checks it. Mendeleev predicted germanium's properties 15 years before it was found.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.random_wrong: Less strongly than it does with iodine

items.q: Sodium burns in chlorine. Xenon is in Group 0, below krypton. Predict what happens when sodium is heated in xenon.
items.correct: No reaction, as xenon is a noble gas
items.misconception: It burns, as xenon is a gas like chlorine
items.why: Weigh up several properties together, and check the element's position: to the right of the staircase line means a non-metal.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.random_wrong: It reacts, as xenon is low in its group

items.q: Which property do all metals have?
items.correct: They can conduct electricity
items.misconception: They are attracted to a magnet
items.why: Being attracted to a magnet is a property of only a few metals; use conductivity, shine and position in the table to identify a metal.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: They are solid at room temperature

items.q: The table shows some properties of four elements. Carbon is a non-metal. Which conclusion does the table support?
items.correct: A non-metal can still conduct electricity
items.misconception: Carbon must be a metal, as it conducts
items.why: Typical properties have exceptions: graphite is a non-metal that conducts, and mercury is a metal that is liquid.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: Iodine is a metal, as it is shiny

items.q: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife and melts at 98 °C. Is sodium a metal, and why?
items.correct: Yes: it is one of the alkali metals
items.misconception: Yes: each sodium atom is soft and shiny
items.why: Keep two levels apart: what you see and measure belongs to a piece of the element; atoms are the tiny particles it is made of.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: No: metals are hard and difficult to melt

items.q: Element W is dull and grey. It conducts electricity, a magnet does not attract it, and it can be hammered flat. What is W, and how can you tell?
items.correct: A metal, as it is malleable and conducts
items.misconception: A metal, as only metals conduct electricity
items.why: Typical properties have exceptions: graphite is a non-metal that conducts, and mercury is a metal that is liquid.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.random_wrong: A non-metal, as it is dull, not shiny

items.q: Sodium oxide and calcium oxide are metal oxides that dissolve in water. What do they form?
items.correct: An alkaline solution
items.misconception: An acidic solution
items.why: Link the oxide to its element: sodium and calcium are metals, and their oxides make alkalis; sulfur is a non-metal, and its oxide helps make acid rain.
items.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
items.random_wrong: Just a neutral solution

items.q: Element X burns in oxygen. Its oxide dissolves in water, making a solution of pH 3. What is X most likely to be?
items.correct: A non-metal, as its oxide is acidic
items.misconception: Either, as all oxides are acidic
items.why: Ask what the oxide is made from: the oxide of a metal such as sodium is a base; the oxide of a non-metal such as sulfur is acidic.
items.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
items.random_wrong: A metal, since metal oxides are acidic

items.q: Copper oxide powder is stirred with water and filtered. The filtered water has pH 7. What is copper oxide?
items.correct: A base, as it can neutralise acids
items.misconception: A neutral oxide, as the water is pH 7
items.why: Indicator only shows what has dissolved. To find out whether an insoluble oxide is a base, see whether it neutralises an acid.
items.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
items.random_wrong: An acidic oxide, like any oxide

items.q: When iodine dissolves in ethanol, is a new substance made?
items.correct: No. Dissolving is a physical change: the iodine spreads out through the ethanol, and evaporating the ethanol gives the iodine back.
items.misconception: Dissolving is a chemical change: the substance that dissolves is turned into something new.
items.why: Dissolving makes a mixture (a solution), not a new substance. The dissolved substance can be got back by evaporating the solvent.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does stirring iron filings and sulfur powder together make a new substance?
items.correct: No. Stirring only mixes them, and each keeps its own properties: a magnet can still pull out the iron. A new substance, iron sulfide, forms only when the mixture is heated and reacts.
items.misconception: Mixing two elements together makes a new substance, so mixing is a chemical change.
items.why: Check whether the parts keep their properties. If they can be separated by a physical method, such as a magnet, they were only mixed.
items.specStatementText: the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Did Mendeleev leave gaps, or swap elements, to make his table look neat?
items.correct: No. His choices followed the properties of the elements: gaps were left for elements not yet discovered, and some elements were swapped so each one sat with elements like it.
items.misconception: Mendeleev's gaps and swaps were there to make his table look neat and even.
items.why: Each gap was a prediction: an element should exist there, with properties like the elements above and below it.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is the periodic table a list of elements in order of reactivity?
items.correct: No. The periodic table orders the elements by atomic number (Mendeleev used atomic mass) and puts similar elements in the same column. The reactivity series is a different list.
items.misconception: The periodic table lists the elements in order of how reactive they are.
items.why: Keep the two apart: the reactivity series ranks metals by reactivity; the periodic table orders elements by atomic number and lines up similar ones in groups.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Did Mendeleev leave a gap for every element discovered after 1869?
items.correct: No. He left gaps only where his pattern showed that an element was missing. He did not know that a whole group, the noble gases, was missing, so his first table had no place for them.
items.misconception: Mendeleev left gaps for all the undiscovered elements, including the noble gases.
items.why: Only a few elements, such as gallium, scandium and germanium, filled Mendeleev's gaps. The noble gases needed a new column.
items.specStatementText: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Which way do the reactivity trends in Groups 1 and 7 go?
items.correct: Going down Group 1, the metals get more reactive. Going down Group 7, the halogens get less reactive.
items.misconception: Reactivity falls going down Group 1 and rises going down Group 7: the two trends are swapped.
items.why: Anchor each trend with an example: potassium bursts into flames on water while lithium only fizzes; chlorine reacts more strongly than iodine.
items.specStatementText: how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Are all metals hard, with high melting points?
items.correct: No. Most are, but sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife and melt below 100 °C, and mercury melts at −39 °C.
items.misconception: All metals are hard and have high melting points.
items.why: Treat typical properties as a guide, not a rule: the Group 1 metals are soft and melt at low temperatures.
items.specStatementText: the properties of metals and non-metals
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does a metal oxide give off hydrogen when it reacts with water, as the metal does?
items.correct: No. Sodium gives off hydrogen with water, but sodium oxide does not: sodium oxide + water → sodium hydroxide, an alkaline solution.
items.misconception: A metal oxide reacts with water in the same way as the metal itself, giving off hydrogen.
items.why: Compare the word equations: sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen, but sodium oxide + water → sodium hydroxide only.
items.specStatementText: the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is every metal oxide an alkali?
items.correct: No. Copper oxide is a base (it neutralises acids) but it does not dissolve in water, so it is not an alkali. An alkali is a base that dissolves, such as sodium oxide.
items.misconception: 'Base' and 'alkali' mean the same thing, so every metal oxide is an alkali.
items.why: Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali: an alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
